zh.question: 火山怎样喷发、造山，又怎样与植物和水相遇？
zh.observe: 从问题进入，不必先选一座具体火山。四个单元依次讨论七个问题：岩浆怎样到达地面、喷发为何不同；物质怎样积成山、海底怎样成山；裸岩怎样长草、凹地怎样留住湖水；地下热怎样加热水。暂停在一个时刻，换镜头追踪同一岩脉、沉积层、地表位点或水路。比较陆地与海底、盾状与成层及渣锥形态时，改变的是当前问题的条件。各问题的进度是各自的教学时钟；一次喷发、长期积山、生态建立和地下水循环不能按同一进度换算真实年数。

academic.title: 贯通与喷发差异：气体、流变和通道
academic.body: 岩浆来自深部岩石的部分熔融；浅部储存区不是所有岩浆的起点，也不是空洞。补给可改变过压，但浮力、围岩应力、构造张裂、脱气和冷却也影响岩脉传播。喷发机制问题选择一次补给驱动的情境：岩脉贯通后才产生本次地表喷出物；停在地下时保留侵入体。比较喷发差异时，岩浆上升引起的降压可让挥发组分出溶、气泡膨胀；流变和气体能否逸出影响溢流、喷泉与碎裂。成分、温度、晶体、供浆及外来水也重要，低黏度不保证没有爆炸，山形也不能唯一决定一次喷发的样式。VEI 主要依据爆炸性喷出物体积并结合喷发柱等证据，不是全部能量、熔岩流量或危险程度的刻度。条形指标和液态纹理均为定性示意，不能推算真实压力、流速或喷发概率。

academic.title: 造山与地表变化：保留下来的物质和不同尺度
academic.body: 熔岩与碎屑在喷发期间累积，山体并非等到熄灭才形成。较易流动的熔岩反复铺展可形成宽缓盾状火山；熔岩与碎屑累积可形成成层火山；喷口附近的火山渣等碎屑可堆起渣锥。大室山是渣锥实例，也曾有山麓熔岩流。陆地和海底是喷发环境，盾状、成层和渣锥是形态分类，草坡和湖泊则涉及地表条件与后续过程，不能当作同一层级的类型。水压、冷却及岩浆与水的相互作用影响水下产物；只有部分海底火山累积足够物质才会出露成岛。生态观察从已经成形的同一山体开始：冷却后，风化颗粒、外来尘土和有机物可逐渐形成基质，种子或孢子还需到达，并有适宜水分与温度。干旱、寒冷、排水快、薄土、新熔岩或厚灰都可延缓或中断建立。没有统一的物种顺序、年数或森林终点；大室山现有草坡还受到传统山烧维护。

academic.title: 湖水与地下热水：凹地、水量平衡和热源
academic.body: 在所选塌陷案例中，岩浆撤出可改变储存区压力及对上覆岩体的支撑；自重仍在的岩体失稳后沿断裂下沉，先形成凹地，再可能积水。这不要求地下留下永久空洞，也不是每次喷发都塌陷。湖泊是否形成还取决于降水、径流、蒸发和渗漏等水量平衡。火山湖装的是水，熔岩湖装的是熔融岩石。湖泊并非一律在火山永久停止后才出现，湖水可与后续喷发或热液活动共存；黄石湖底就有热液出流。地下热水问题追踪另一条水路：降水补给的地下水沿连通孔隙与裂隙循环，经热岩石加热后可能上升出露。火山区的热源可包括岩浆或仍热的侵入岩，但并非所有温泉都源于火山，深循环水也能由随深度升温的岩石加热。喷气、温泉、植被和湖水都不能单独判定下一次喷发或永久熄灭；休眠与熄灭判断还需地质年代、构造、供浆史和监测证据。

zh.misconception: 没有所有火山共同的“喷发—熄灭—长草—成湖—温泉”顺序。陆海环境、山体形态、植被、湖泊和热液活动回答不同问题；它们可以在不同条件下组合。
zh.boundary: 七个问题是互相衔接的概念观察，不是同一火山连续实测的一生。各问题有独立的压缩教学进度；一次喷发、长期堆积、生态建立、水量平衡与地下水循环没有共同真实时标。剖面、层厚、储存深度、碎屑、土层和根系的尺度，以及熔岩纹理、气泡和水路运动都为辨认而示意；液态细节可单独暂停，不据此读取实测深度、速度、温度或喷发时刻。这些情境也不用于危险预测。

narration.label: 单元一：岩浆怎样到达地面
narration.text: 先问一个问题：岩浆为什么会来到地面？跟着地下同一条裂缝，看岩浆向上走。有时路通了，地面才出现熔岩和碎屑；有时岩浆停在地下。再问：为什么喷出来的样子不同？有的熔岩流开，有的像喷泉，有的带出许多火山灰。气泡、岩浆的稠稀和通道都会影响结果，遇到水也可能改变过程。先跟路径，再比较条件。
narration.cue: 进入“为什么会喷发”，暂停追踪同一岩脉尖端；比较贯通与停滞。转到“喷发为什么不同”，分别观察熔岩流、喷泉与富灰喷发。两个问题各用自己的进度，不把不同结果拼成一场实测喷发。

narration.label: 单元二：留下的物质怎样造山
narration.text: 喷出来的东西去了哪里？熔岩铺在地面，碎屑落回坡上，冷却后留下来。新的物质再盖上去，山才一点点积高、积宽。宽缓的盾状火山、成层火山和渣锥，记录了不同的堆积。大室山是渣锥的一个例子。海底也会积山，不过海水改变了压力和冷却。有些山能长出海面，有些一直留在水下。山形和陆海环境，是两种不同的比较。
narration.cue: 在“山怎样堆起来”中追踪喷口、飞行碎屑、落地转暗和保留的沉积；在问题内比较盾状、成层和渣锥。进入“海底怎样成山”，比较水下积山与有条件出露，不把成岛设成必然终点。

narration.label: 单元三：裸岩、草坡与湖水
narration.text: 山留下了，地表还会改变。先看裸岩怎样长草：岩石冷却，细土和水被留住，种子来到合适的地方，才能扎根。换成干旱、寒冷或厚灰覆盖，再看同一处。大室山今天的草坡，还有人们长期山烧维护。再问湖水从哪里来：有凹地，还要有水进入、留得住，才可能成湖。草坡不必接着变成湖，湖泊也不证明火山已经永久熄灭。
narration.cue: 生态问题从已成形的同一山体开始，追踪固定地表位点，保持进度比较四种环境；再进入独立的湖泊问题，依次观察成盆与水量平衡。说明湖泊可与热液活动共存，两问不是同一座山的必经下一步。

narration.label: 单元四：地下热怎样遇到水
narration.text: 地面没有熔岩流出来，地下也可能还很热。雨水渗进岩石缝隙，遇到热岩石，被加热后又沿连通的路往上走，可能形成温泉。水走的路和岩浆走的路，要分开追踪。湖底也可能有热水流出。并不是每一处温泉都来自火山，有些水在地下走得很深，被那里较热的岩石加热。看到热水，我们还要问：水从哪里来，热从哪里来？
narration.cue: 进入“地下热与水”，先辨认降水补给、渗流路径、热岩区和出流口，再跟踪同一水路。液态运动为示意并可独立暂停；不标注未经校准的深度、速度或循环年数，也不把热液放在所有火山的最后一阶段。

en.question: How do volcanoes erupt, build land, and interact with plants and water?
en.observe: Start with a question; you do not need to choose a named volcano first. Four units connect seven questions: how magma reaches the surface and why eruptions differ; how deposits build mountains on land and under the sea; how bare rock supports plants and how depressions retain lakes; and how underground heat warms water. Pause at a moment and follow the same dike, deposit, surface site or water pathway through different views. Land versus sea and shield, composite and scoria-cone forms are conditions compared within a question. Each question has its own teaching clock: one eruption, long-term accumulation, ecological establishment and groundwater circulation cannot share a conversion from progress to years.

academic.title: Connection and eruption differences: gas, flow and pathways
academic.body: Magma originates through partial melting at depth; shallow storage is neither the origin of all magma nor an empty cavern. Recharge can change overpressure, while buoyancy, host-rock stress, tectonic extension, degassing and cooling also influence dike propagation. The mechanism question selects one recharge-driven episode: this episode produces surface ejecta only after the dike connects to the surface; a stalled intrusion remains underground. In the eruption comparison, falling pressure during ascent can let volatiles exsolve and bubbles expand. Flow properties and gas escape affect effusion, fountains and fragmentation. Composition, temperature, crystals, supply and external water also matter. Low viscosity does not rule out explosions, and mountain shape does not uniquely determine an eruption style. VEI primarily uses explosive ejecta volume together with plume evidence; it is not a scale for all energy, lava discharge or hazard. Bars and moving liquid textures are qualitative illustrations, not measurements of pressure, flow speed or eruption probability.

academic.title: Building land and changing surfaces: retained material at different scales
academic.body: Lava and fragments accumulate during eruptions; extinction does not create the mountain. Repeated fluid lava flows can build a broad shield, lava and fragment deposits can build a composite volcano, and scoria deposited around a vent can build a scoria cone. Omuroyama is a scoria-cone example that also produced lava from its foot. Land and sea are eruption environments; shield, composite and scoria cone describe forms; grassland and lakes concern surface conditions and subsequent processes. These are different comparisons, not peer categories. Water pressure, cooling and magma–water interaction influence submarine products. Only some submarine volcanoes accumulate enough material to emerge as islands. The ecology question starts on the same already formed mountain: after cooling, weathered grains, windblown dust and organic material may build substrate. Seeds or spores must also arrive, with suitable moisture and temperature. Drought, cold, rapid drainage, thin soil, new lava or thick ash may delay or interrupt establishment. There is no universal species sequence, fixed number of years or inevitable forest endpoint. Traditional burning also maintains Omuroyama’s present grassland.

academic.title: Lake water and hot groundwater: basins, water balance and heat sources
academic.body: In the selected collapse example, magma withdrawal changes storage pressure and support for overlying rock. Its weight remains, and unstable rock may subside along faults, creating a depression before water can collect. This requires no permanent underground cavern, and not every eruption causes collapse. Lake formation also depends on precipitation, runoff, evaporation and leakage. Volcanic lakes contain water; lava lakes contain molten rock. Lakes do not all wait for permanent extinction: lake water may coexist with later eruptions or hydrothermal activity, and Yellowstone Lake has hydrothermal discharge on its floor. The underground-heat question follows another pathway. Groundwater supplied by precipitation circulates through connected pores and fractures, gains heat from hot rock and may rise to discharge at the surface. In volcanic areas the heat source can include magma or still-hot intrusions. However, not every hot spring has a volcanic heat source: deep circulation can heat water in rocks that become warmer with depth. Gas emissions, hot springs, vegetation and lakes cannot individually establish the next eruption or permanent extinction. Dormancy and extinction assessments also need geological ages, tectonic setting, magma-supply history and monitoring evidence.

en.misconception: There is no universal eruption–extinction–grassland–lake–hot-spring sequence. Land or sea, mountain form, vegetation, lakes and hydrothermal activity answer different questions and can occur in different combinations.
en.boundary: The seven connected questions are conceptual observations, not a measured continuous life history of one volcano. Each has an independent compressed teaching progress. One eruption, long-term deposition, ecological establishment, water balance and groundwater circulation have no common calibrated timescale. Cutaways, bed thicknesses, storage depths, clasts, soil and roots are scaled for recognition; lava textures, bubbles and moving water paths are illustrative too. Liquid details can be paused separately. They do not provide measured depth, speed, temperature or eruption timing, and these scenarios are not hazard forecasts.

narration.label: Unit one: how magma reaches the surface
narration.text: Start with a question: why does magma reach the surface? Follow the same underground crack as magma moves upward. Sometimes the path connects and lava and fragments appear above ground. Sometimes magma stops below. Then ask why eruptions look different. Some lava spreads out, some rises in fountains, and some eruptions carry abundant ash. Bubbles, how readily magma flows, and its pathway all affect the result. Encountering water can change the process too. Follow the path, then compare the conditions.
narration.cue: Open Why does it erupt and pause to follow the same dike tip. Compare connection with a stalled intrusion. Move to Why do eruptions differ and observe a lava flow, fountains and an ash-rich eruption. The two questions have separate progress; their outcomes are not one measured eruption.

narration.label: Unit two: how retained material builds land
narration.text: Where does erupted material go? Lava spreads across the ground, fragments land on slopes, and cooled material stays. New deposits accumulate above it, gradually raising and widening the mountain. Broad shields, composite volcanoes and scoria cones record different deposits. Omuroyama is one scoria-cone example. Mountains also grow under the sea, where water changes pressure and cooling. Some emerge above the sea; others remain submerged. Mountain shape and land or sea are two different comparisons.
narration.cue: In How do mountains build up, follow the vent, flying fragments, darkening landings and retained deposits. Compare shield, composite and scoria-cone forms inside that question. Open How do mountains grow underwater to compare submerged growth and conditional emergence; an island is not an inevitable endpoint.

narration.label: Unit three: bare rock, grassland and lakes
narration.text: The mountain remains, but its surface can change. First follow how bare rock supports grass. Rock cools, fine material and water collect, and arriving seeds need a suitable place to root. Try dry, cold or thick-ash conditions at the same site. People’s traditional burning also maintains Omuroyama’s grassland today. Next ask where lake water comes from. A depression needs incoming water and a way to retain it. Grassland need not become a lake, and a lake does not prove that a volcano is permanently extinct.
narration.cue: Begin ecology on the same already formed mountain. Follow fixed surface sites and retain progress while comparing four environments. Then open the separate lake question, observing basin formation before water balance. Explain that lakes can coexist with hydrothermal activity; neither question is a mandatory next step for one mountain.

narration.label: Unit four: how underground heat meets water
narration.text: Even without lava flowing above ground, rock below can remain hot. Rainwater enters cracks, gains heat from hot rock, and may rise through connected pathways to form a hot spring. Follow the water path separately from the magma path. Hot water can also flow from a lake bed. Not every hot spring comes from a volcano. Some water circulates deep enough to be warmed by hotter rock below. Whenever we see hot water, we can ask two questions: where did the water come from, and where did the heat come from?
narration.cue: Open Underground heat and water. Identify precipitation recharge, permeable pathways, the hot-rock zone and discharge, then follow the same water route. Liquid movement is illustrative and can be paused independently. Give no uncalibrated depths, speeds or circulation ages, and do not place hydrothermal activity at the end of every volcanic history.
